newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Foncier siege goes on, talks at 0930 GMT.
newsitem.headline: Credit Foncier siege goes on, talks at 0930 GMT.

text.p: The staff siege of French property lender Credit Foncier entered a fifth day on Tuesday with the chairman still captive at the Paris headquarters but talks between unions and a go-between set for 0930 GMT.
"For the moment there's no question of a plan to end the occupation or the holding of Mr Meyssonnier," one of the staff union representatives, Claude Dubeau, told Reuters.
About three hundred people were in the central lobby of the plush Paris headquarters early on Tuesday morning, many of them having spent the night there, he said.
Dubeau said the cross-union negotiating team would meet at 0800 GMT before talks at 0930 GMT with Philippe Rouvillois, the government-appointed go-between.

"We are going there with an open mind but it's clear that we are not going in there to just hear an explanation of the Arthuis plan," he said, referring to the break-up of Credit Foncier announced by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis in July.
Dubeau said it was impossible to tell how long talks would last and that the union negotiators would meet again after the talks with Rouvillois, formerly head of France's SNCF state railways.

Arthuis repeated on Monday evening that there was currently no alternative to a proposed takeover of Credit Foncier's property loans portfolio and some 1,500 members of the 3,000 staff by cooperative group Credit Immobilier.
The rest of the organisation would be spun off into a state holding company, effectively winding up Credit Foncier which was established by Emperor Napoleon III 145 years ago.

Although Arthuis says he has no hard-and-fast plan, he has already "nationalised" Credit Foncier via a takeover of the home loans group by state-owned bank Caisses des Depots as a prelude to the wind-down.

Jacques Guillet, a member of the RPR party which is the senior partner in France's ruling centre-right coalition, issued a statement on Monday evening saying that, since the group had been taken over by a state bank, France's privatisation commission would have to be consulted on any future moves.

Guillet has long been campaigning along with deputies from both sides of the parliamentary divide, for the government to seek an alternative to the shut-down plan that was announced after Credit Foncier reported 1995 losses of nearly 11 billion francs.

Guillet highlighted the predictions by Credit Foncier boss of a profit of one billion francs in 1996 and said the 1995 accounts should be reexamined to assess whether the group was viable, as the unions claim, or not, as the government says.
